passage: I'm Kavitha, and I share the open-plan office with Usha, who manages our team. On Monday Usha sent Bhavna a one-line message: “Prepare the vendor summary by Wednesday.” Bhavna spent two days on a twelve-page comparison with charts. On Wednesday, Usha opened it, and her jaw tightened. “I wanted one page, for the board. This is a report.” Bhavna said quietly, “I didn't know it was for the board.” Usha sighed loudly and later muttered to me, “Some people just don't listen.” I couldn't say what Usha was feeling; maybe stress. But I remember that the message had no audience, no length and no purpose.

qa.q: By which day was the vendor summary due?
qa.a: The vendor summary was due by Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Usha have been feeling when her jaw tightened?
qa.a: Usha was probably frustrated and stressed, and blamed Bhavna for not listening, though Kavitha cannot see the inner state exactly.

qa.q: What could Usha do differently when handing over the next task?
qa.a: Say who the summary is for, how long it should be, what it is for and when it is due, and agree a quick check on Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel after two days of work and Usha's reaction?
qa.a: Bhavna probably feels confused and disheartened, since the effort was real and the one-line message did not say the audience.

grounding: A manager hands a task off with one line, expects the result in their head, and blames the person when it differs.

passage:
Monday: Dolma sent Bhavna a one-line message before a meeting: “Sort the client feedback.” Bhavna wasn't sure whether sort meant summarise, tag or reply, so she made a spreadsheet of sixty rows and sent it Tuesday night.

Wednesday: Dolma opened the file, sighed and said, “This is not what I meant. I needed the top three complaints.” Bhavna's face fell. “I didn't know that.” Dolma turned away and said, more sharply than she intended, “I don't know how else to say it.”

Friday: Dolma told a colleague, “I explained it, and she still got it wrong.”

qa.q: How many rows did Bhavna's spreadsheet have?
qa.a: Bhavna's spreadsheet had sixty rows.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when saying “I don't know how else to say it”?
qa.a: Dolma was irritated and frustrated, believing the instruction was clear; the sharp tone shows Dolma blames the person, though the message was the gap.

qa.q: What could Dolma do on Monday to prevent this result?
qa.a: Write what she wants, the top three complaints and who will read it, and say when it is due and when they will look at it together.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when her face fell on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bhavna was probably confused and dismayed, since she had worked hard on a guess at what “sort” meant.

grounding: A person passes on a task with one line, expects it to match what was in their head and blames the other person when it does not.

passage:
Karthik: Minakshi, did you finish the market summary?
Minakshi: yes! sent it this morning
Karthik: this isn't what I needed
Minakshi: oh. what did you need?
Karthik: I wanted a one-page comparison of our three competitors, with prices
Minakshi: your message just said "can you do a market summary"
Karthik: well, obviously for the board meeting
Minakshi: I didn't know it was for the board. I wrote a general 5-page overview 😰
Karthik: this is really frustrating. the meeting's tomorrow
Minakshi: I can redo it tonight
Karthik: (after a while) actually, that's on me. I didn't say any of that
Karthik: one page, 3 competitors, prices, by 11 tomorrow. sorry
Minakshi: got it. thanks for explaining

qa.q: How many pages was Minakshi's overview?
qa.a: Minakshi wrote a general 5-page overview.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling on writing "this isn't what I needed"?
qa.a: Karthik felt frustrated and let down, expecting the result to match an unspoken picture.

qa.q: What did Karthik realise, and what could change next time?
qa.a: Karthik realised the one-line instruction was the gap; next time the purpose, length, content and deadline should be stated up front.

qa.q: How does Minakshi experience the exchange?
qa.a: Minakshi feels anxious and confused, having done what the message said without knowing it was for the board.

grounding: A chat shows a manager passing on a task in one line, blaming the result, then recognising that the instruction was the gap.

passage: Maria ran a small health-awareness NGO in a town near Thrissur. Before the district meeting, she told her new coordinator Rashmi, "Make a poster for the camp." Nothing else. Rashmi designed a bright poster with the date and a cartoon doctor. Maria looked at it and her jaw tightened. "Where's the list of free tests? The Malayalam text? The phone number? This is for the panchayat board, not children." Rashmi's face fell. "You didn't tell me any of that." Maria started to answer, then stopped. She had pictured the whole poster in her head for weeks and assumed Rashmi could see it too. "You're right. Let's sit for ten minutes and I'll tell you everything I meant."

qa.q: What did Rashmi put on the first poster?
qa.a: A bright poster with the date and a cartoon doctor.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she first saw the poster?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and frustrated, her jaw tightening, because it didn't match what she had pictured.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Maria do about it?
qa.a: Maria gave a one-line instruction and expected Rashmi to read her mind; she fixed it by sitting down to explain everything she meant.

qa.q: How does Rashmi feel when Maria lists what is missing?
qa.a: Rashmi feels deflated and unfairly blamed, since none of those details were given.

grounding: Shows a manager passing on a one-line task, being frustrated by the result, then realising the instruction was the gap.

passage: Chen managed a small logistics team in Singapore. On Monday, he emailed his new analyst Priscila: "Please look into delivery delays." On Thursday she sent back a detailed report on weather patterns and delays across five years. Chen read it and felt his temper rise. He'd wanted a list of the last month's late deliveries, sorted by driver, for a meeting tomorrow. He started typing a sharp reply: "This isn't useful." Then he read his own Monday email again. Six words. No purpose, no deadline, no format. He deleted the reply. Instead he called her. "Your report is thorough. My request was vague. Here's what I actually need, by noon tomorrow."

qa.q: How many years did Priscila's report cover?
qa.a: It covered five years.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when he started typing the sharp reply?
qa.a: He felt his temper rising, angry that the report didn't match what he had wanted.

qa.q: What made Chen change his reply, and why was that wise?
qa.a: Re-reading his own six-word email showed the instruction was the gap, so calling Priscila with clear details was fairer and more useful.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel after Chen's call?
qa.a: Priscila might feel relieved and respected, since her effort was acknowledged and she now knows what is needed.

grounding: Shows a manager whose one-line request produced the wrong result, and who sees that the vague instruction, not the person, was the gap.

passage: On Friday, Tanvir, manager of the Chembur cricket academy, messaged Darshan between two parent meetings: "Sort out the kit room before Monday." In Tanvir's head, that meant counting the helmets, setting aside the cracked ones, and listing what to order before the new batch of forty under-12s arrived. On Monday he opened the kit room door. It gleamed. Pads were stacked by size, bats hung on new hooks, the floor was mopped. There was no list. "Where's the count? What do we order?" Tanvir said, loud enough for the ground staff to hear. "You had all weekend." Darshan went red. "You said sort it out. I sorted it." Tanvir walked off muttering about people who don't think ahead. That night he scrolled back to his message. Seven words. He read it twice.

qa.q: How many under-12s were joining the academy?
qa.a: A new batch of forty under-12s.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have been feeling as he read his message twice that night?
qa.a: He was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed, starting to see that the gap was in his seven words, not in Darshan's effort.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have written on Friday instead?
qa.a: He could have said what the job was for and what he needed back: count the helmets, set aside cracked ones, and send a list of what to order before the new batch.

qa.q: How was the Monday exchange for Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan had worked hard all weekend and was then scolded in front of the ground staff, so it was humiliating and felt unfair.

grounding: Shows a manager who hands over a task in one vague line, is angry when the result differs from what he imagined, and blames the other person.
